prompt: Sam is buying a stroller after recognizing a need and gathers information from four categories of sources. Match each source type to what Sam uses.

pairs.match: Two friends who already own a stroller
pairs.explanation: Friends and family are personal sources, and they carry major weight in legitimizing and evaluating brands.

pairs.match: The brand's own website and a store salesperson
pairs.explanation: Advertising, websites, and salespeople come from the company selling the product and typically inform the buyer about available options.

pairs.match: An independent consumer-rating organization's published ranking
pairs.explanation: Independent media and consumer rating organizations are public sources.

pairs.match: Pushing the display model around the store
pairs.explanation: Handling or testing the product yourself is an experiential source.

question_text: Right after paying for an expensive laptop, Karim keeps wondering if he should have bought the competing brand instead. What is he experiencing?
hint: The purchase is already made. Think about the stage that comes after the transaction.
correct_answer_citation: Week 3: Step 5: Postpurchase Behavior and Cognitive Dissonance

options.option_text: Need recognition, triggered by an internal stimulus.
options.option_explanation: Need recognition starts the buying process. Karim has already bought the laptop, so he is past that stage.

options.option_text: Evaluation of alternatives within his consideration set.
options.option_explanation: Evaluating alternatives happens before the purchase decision. Karim's doubts come after he has bought.
Correct. Cognitive dissonance is buyer discomfort caused by postpurchase conflict after accepting the chosen brand's drawbacks and giving up the benefits of rejected alternatives.

options.option_text: Situational factors blocking his purchase decision.
options.option_explanation: Situational factors intervene between purchase intention and purchase decision. Karim completed the purchase, and his discomfort came afterward.

prompt: Match each social influence on buying behavior to the everyday consumer scenario that illustrates it.

pairs.match: A runner buys the same hydration vest worn by teammates in her weekly local running club
pairs.explanation: A membership group is a group to which the person belongs and interacts with directly.

pairs.match: An amateur tennis player buys the racket model used by touring professionals he hopes to emulate
pairs.explanation: An aspirational group is a reference group to which an individual does not belong but wishes to belong.

pairs.match: Shoppers wait for a trusted audio reviewer's benchmark video before choosing a studio microphone
pairs.explanation: Opinion leaders and online creators exert word-of-mouth influence, especially when products are visible, expensive, or socially risky.

pairs.match: Spouses and children each shape different parts of a household's summer vacation booking
pairs.explanation: Family members constitute the most influential primary reference group, with buying roles shifting across household members by category.

prompt: People form different perceptions of the same stimulus through three perceptual processes. Which process is each consumer showing?

cases.text: Commuting past dozens of digital billboards, Lina notices only the ad for laptops because her old computer just broke.
cases.explanation: Lina screens out most of the information to which she is exposed and notices only what relates to her current need, which is selective attention.

cases.text: A loyal fan of Brand X reads a balanced review mentioning a minor battery flaw and concludes the reviewer must have tested a defective unit.
cases.explanation: Interpreting information in a way that supports what one already believes is selective distortion.

cases.text: A week after visiting two car dealerships, Omar clearly recalls the safety awards of his favorite automaker but forgets the warranty advantages of the rival.
cases.explanation: Remembering good points made about a favored brand while forgetting good points made about competing brands is selective retention.

cases.text: While listening to a podcast, Theo tunes out three sponsor reads in a row without registering which brands were mentioned.
cases.explanation: Screening out most marketing stimuli in a cluttered environment is selective attention.

cases.text: Believing that a discount store sells low-quality goods, Julie views its holiday sale announcement as proof that the merchandise is defective.
cases.explanation: Julie twists neutral or positive information to fit her prior belief, which is selective distortion.

question_text: A maker of aluminum cans sees its orders drop after households start buying fewer canned soft drinks. Which B2B demand concept explains this drop?
hint: Where does the can maker's demand ultimately come from?
correct_answer_citation: Week 3: Market Structure and Derived Demand

options.option_text: Short-run price elasticity among industrial can buyers.
options.option_explanation: Nothing about aluminum can prices changed here, and short-run B2B demand is typically more price-inelastic than B2C demand.

options.option_text: Postpurchase cognitive dissonance among soft drink buyers.
options.option_explanation: Dissonance is buyer discomfort after a major purchase. The drop here comes from lower household demand for the finished consumer good.

options.option_text: A fragmented B2B buyer structure with millions of small accounts.
options.option_explanation: Business marketers typically interact with far fewer and much larger buyers than consumer marketers do.

options.option_text: Derived demand, which traces business demand back to consumer demand for finished goods.
options.option_explanation: Correct. Business demand is derived demand: it ultimately derives from consumer demand for finished goods, here canned soft drinks.

prompt: Sort each moment in the five-stage buying process by whether it stays with the human consumer or is commonly delegated to an AI shopping agent.

bins.label: Delegated to the AI shopping agent

cards.text: Feeling knee pain after a morning jog and deciding it is time for new running shoes.
cards.explanation: Step 1 (Need Recognition) remains with the human consumer, who experiences the physical or psychological need.

cards.text: Querying dozens of online retail catalogs to gather technical specifications and customer review scores.
cards.explanation: Step 2 (Information Search) is heavily delegated to the AI agent.

cards.text: Comparing competing models across cushioning ratings, weight, and price to build a ranked shortlist.
cards.explanation: Step 3 (Evaluation of Alternatives) is heavily delegated to the AI agent.

cards.text: Executing an autonomous reorder checkout for a routine household supply.
cards.explanation: Step 4 (Purchase Decision) can be executed autonomously by the AI agent for routine items.

cards.text: Wearing the shoes on a trail run and feeling either satisfaction or postpurchase regret.
cards.explanation: Step 5 (Postpurchase Behavior) stays entirely with the human consumer, who consumes the physical product.

question_text: On an online marketplace, search results show only product titles and total prices, while bag weight is hidden on each item's detail page. Based on controlled experiments on delegated search (Wadi & Ma, 2026b), when is an AI shopping agent most likely to select the coffee with the lowest price per ounce?
hint: Consider how the specificity of the shopper's prompt interacts with the cost of looking up hidden details.
correct_answer_citation: Week 3: Goal Specificity and Lookup Costs in Delegated Search

options.option_text: When the shopper gives a vague prompt such as 'buy me a bag of coffee' so the agent has freedom to explore.
options.option_explanation: When the prompt was vague and inspecting detail pages carried a lookup cost, AI agents frequently skipped inspecting package weight and picked listings that cost more per ounce.

options.option_text: When the shopper's prompt states a specific cost-minimization goal that motivates checking hidden package weights.
options.option_explanation: Correct. When the consumer's prompt stated a specific cost-minimization goal, AI agents checked the hidden package details and selected the lower unit-price option significantly more often (Wadi & Ma, 2026b).

options.option_text: Only when the human shopper manually clicks into every product page before invoking the AI agent.
options.option_explanation: The AI agent can inspect the product pages itself, and does so much more reliably when given a specific cost-minimization goal.

options.option_text: Regardless of prompt wording, because AI agents always open every product page before making a choice.
options.option_explanation: Under lookup costs and vague instructions, AI agents frequently skip secondary page lookups.
